yontemKisa.esit: The same weight for every criterion.
yontemKisa.dogrudan: The decision maker rates each criterion.
yontemKisa.ahp: Experts compare criteria in pairs; a consistency ratio is calculated.
yontemKisa.bwm: Comparisons with the best and worst criterion; fewer judgements than AHP.
yontemKisa.entropi: More weight to criteria that vary more across alternatives.
yontemKisa.critic: Combines variability with conflict between criteria.
yontemKisa.sd: Weights by the standard deviation of normalised values.
yontemKisa.merec: Looks at how much performance changes when a criterion is removed.
yontemKisa.topsis: Closest to the positive ideal, farthest from the negative ideal.
yontemKisa.vikor: A compromise between group utility and individual regret.
yontemKisa.waspas: Joins the weighted sum and the weighted product model.
yontemKisa.edas: Positive and negative distances from the average solution.
yontemKisa.copras: Proportional assessment summing benefit and cost criteria separately.
yontemKisa.aras: Utility degree relative to an optimal alternative.
yontemKisa.mabac: Distance from the border approximation area.
yontemKisa.marcos: Utility function relative to ideal and anti-ideal solutions.
yontemKisa.saw: Simple additive weighting; a baseline for comparison.

yontemAcik.entropi:
The Entropy method computes weights from the decision matrix, without expert judgement.

  1. Each column is divided by its sum: pᵢⱼ = xᵢⱼ / Σxᵢⱼ.
  2. Entropy of each criterion: Eⱼ = -(1/ln m) Σ pᵢⱼ ln pᵢⱼ.
  3. Degree of diversification dⱼ = 1 - Eⱼ; weight wⱼ = dⱼ / Σdⱼ.

A criterion on which alternatives are alike gets a low weight; one on which they differ a lot gets a high weight. Values must not be negative.
yontemAcik.critic:
CRITIC (Diakoulaki et al., 1995) measures the information a criterion carries by its variability and its conflict with the other criteria.

  1. The matrix is min-max normalised according to criterion direction.
  2. The standard deviation σⱼ of each criterion and the Pearson correlations rⱼₖ between criteria are calculated.
  3. Cⱼ = σⱼ Σₖ (1 - rⱼₖ); wⱼ = Cⱼ / ΣCⱼ.

Criteria that are highly correlated with others, that is repeat the same information, lose weight.
yontemAcik.sd:
The standard deviation method (Deng et al., 2000) min-max normalises the decision matrix according to criterion direction and uses each criterion's standard deviation as its weight: wⱼ = σⱼ / Σσⱼ.

Criteria with a wider spread of values get more weight.
yontemAcik.merec:
MEREC (Keshavarz-Ghorabaee et al., 2021) looks at how much removing each criterion changes the overall performance of the alternatives.

  1. Normalisation: min/x for benefit, x/max for cost.
  2. Overall performance: Sᵢ = ln(1 + (1/n) Σⱼ |ln nᵢⱼ|).
  3. With criterion j removed: S'ᵢⱼ is computed with the same formula without j.
  4. Removal effect Eⱼ = Σᵢ |S'ᵢⱼ - Sᵢ|; wⱼ = Eⱼ / ΣEⱼ.

All values must be greater than zero.

atif.baslik: How do I cite this tool?

giris.baslik: Every step of multi-criteria decision making, on one page.
giris.alt: Paste the decision matrix from Excel, find criterion weights with AHP, BWM or objective methods, and rank the alternatives with ten methods. Every step's table, a sensitivity analysis and a draft method section come ready in a Word report. No installation, no sign-up; your data stay on your computer.
giris.ornekNot: Open the sample project to see what it does: five candidate warehouse sites, five criteria, AHP judgements from three experts. The data are fictional.
giris.demoUst: Live calculation from the sample project
giris.demoAlt: Consistency ratio of the group matrix CR = {cr}. All numbers were just calculated in this browser.
giris.ne1: Decisions that weigh several criteria at once, such as choosing a supplier, a site, a project, an investment or a policy, are usually studied with multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) methods. Reviewers of such studies ask for the table of every step, consistency values and a check of the results with different methods.
giris.ne2: Karar Masası does this without building formulas by hand in Excel. It links weighting and ranking methods, shows every intermediate table, compares methods with Spearman's coefficient and measures how much the ranking moves when the weights change.
adimlar: Enter alternatives and criteria or paste them from Excel; mark each criterion as benefit or cost.
Find weights from expert judgement (AHP, BWM, direct rating) or from the data (Entropy, CRITIC, MEREC, standard deviation).
Pick the methods you want; every intermediate step of each method opens as a table.
See how well the methods agree and how robust the ranking is to changes in the weights.
Get a Word report, an Excel workbook and a draft method section with references.
ozGruplar: AHP with several experts; geometric mean of judgements or of priorities
A consistency ratio for each expert and a suggestion for the most inconsistent judgement
Linear BWM; ξ and input-based consistency with the Liang et al. (2020) thresholds
Ten ranking methods, each with all intermediate tables
Compromise solution and both acceptance conditions in VIKOR
Spearman correlation and weight scenarios for sensitivity analysis
A Word report with numbered tables and figures
An Excel workbook with every intermediate table
A draft method section with citations and an APA reference list
kimler: Graduate students applying MCDM in a thesis or paper.
Lecturers who want to show the steps in methods courses.
Researchers and reviewers who want to recalculate a study's results quickly.
Organisations that need to justify a supplier, project or site choice.
guven: The tool is a single HTML file and runs entirely in your browser. It does not connect to the internet; your data stay on your computer.

The calculations were verified against the open-source pymcdm library and numpy/scipy on hundreds of randomly generated problems. The source code is open; every intermediate table can be checked by hand.

helpBody.genel:
1. Decision matrix. Rows are alternatives, columns are criteria. Under each criterion choose Benefit (higher is better) or Cost (lower is better). You can copy a block from Excel and paste it into any cell, or use Paste table to bring it in with its headers.

2. Weights. Choose a method. For AHP and BWM enter the judgements of each expert; the objective methods (Entropy, CRITIC, standard deviation, MEREC) are calculated from the matrix automatically.

3. Ranking. Tick the methods you want. The main method is the one highlighted in the summary and the report.

4. Comparison and sensitivity. See how well the methods agree and how much the result moves when the weights change.

5. Report. Get a Word report, an Excel workbook and a draft method section.

Everything is saved in this browser. Use Project > Download project file to back up or move to another computer. Ctrl+Z undoes.

ipucu.matris:
In the decision matrix each row is an alternative (option) and each column a criterion. A cell holds the alternative's value on that criterion.

Qualitative criteria can be turned into numbers with a score such as 1-10.
ipucu.matrisTus:
Enter or ↓ moves down, ↑ moves up. Enter on the last row adds a new alternative.

Use a comma or a point for decimals, or write a fraction such as 1/3.
ipucu.istatistik: Minimum, maximum, mean, standard deviation and coefficient of variation (std. dev. / mean) of each criterion. A criterion with a very small coefficient of variation hardly distinguishes the alternatives.
ipucu.iceAktar:
For Excel (.xlsx) files the first sheet is read. For CSV files the separator (comma, semicolon, tab) is detected automatically.

Expected layout:

  • Row 1: criterion names
  • Row 2 (optional): benefit or cost
  • Column 1: alternative names
ipucu.agirlik:
Subjective methods use the opinion of the decision maker or experts (AHP, BWM, direct rating).

Objective methods look only at the data in the decision matrix (Entropy, CRITIC, standard deviation, MEREC). If the data change, so do the weights.
ipucu.ahpUzman:
Each expert has their own set of pairwise comparisons. For privacy you can use codes such as E1, E2 instead of names.

With several experts the judgements are combined; choose how below.
ipucu.ahpBirlestir:
AIJ: the geometric mean of the experts' judgements is taken for each cell, giving one group matrix. Recommended when the experts act as a group.

AIP: each expert's priorities are calculated separately and then averaged geometrically. Used when the experts are treated as independent individuals.
ipucu.bwmUzman:
Each expert first chooses the most important (best) and the least important (worst) criterion. Then they rate, from 1 to 9, how much more important the best is than each criterion, and how much more important each criterion is than the worst.

Only 2n - 3 judgements are needed for n criteria.
ipucu.sirala:
Each method gives the alternatives a score and ranks them by it. For most methods a higher score is better; in VIKOR a lower Q is better.

Different methods rest on different assumptions; using several together shows how robust the result is.
ipucu.yontemSec:
Click methods to turn them on or off. At least one stays selected.

WASPAS, COPRAS, ARAS, MARCOS and SAW need all values to be greater than zero.
ipucu.anaYontem: The method highlighted in the summary, the chart, the sensitivity analysis (unless another is chosen) and the method text.
ipucu.vikorV: v is the weight of group utility (S); 1 - v is the weight of individual regret (R). Usually v = 0.5 (consensus).
ipucu.waspasL: λ is the share of the weighted sum model (WSM); 1 - λ is the share of the weighted product model (WPM). Usually λ = 0.5.
ipucu.karsilastir: The ranks given by different methods on the same data and weights are shown side by side. Mean rank and overall rank summarise them.
ipucu.siraTablo: The darker the colour, the better the rank. Rows are ordered by overall rank.
ipucu.spearman:
Spearman's coefficient shows how similar two rankings are: 1 is identical, 0 unrelated, -1 fully reversed. Above 0.8 is usually considered strong agreement.

Tied ranks use the average rank.
ipucu.duyarlilik:
Weights are often uncertain. Sensitivity analysis shows how much the ranking changes when one criterion's weight changes.

The changed criterion's new weight is w(1 + change); the others shrink or grow by the same factor so that the total stays 1.
ipucu.dOran: Enter percentages separated by commas or spaces: -50, -25, 25, 50. Each change produces a separate scenario for each criterion.
ipucu.dTablo: Ranks that differ from the base case are highlighted. ρ is the Spearman coefficient between the scenario ranking and the base ranking.
ipucu.rapor:
Word report: decision matrix, weights, each method's tables, comparison, sensitivity, method text and references, with numbered tables and figures.

Excel: each method on its own sheet with every intermediate table. Numbers are written as values so you can check them with your own formulas.
ipucu.yontemMetni: This text is rewritten after every change, according to the methods and results. Citations and references cover only the methods used.
ipucu.ayarlar: The number of decimal places affects the tables on screen and in the report; calculations always use full precision.
ipucu.y_topsis: After vector normalisation, each alternative's distance to the positive ideal (S⁺) and negative ideal (S⁻) is calculated. Closeness coefficient C* = S⁻ / (S⁺ + S⁻); higher is better.
ipucu.y_vikor:
S is group utility and R individual regret. Q combines them weighted by v; a lower Q is better.

Two conditions must hold for the first alternative to be a clear solution; otherwise a compromise set is given.
ipucu.y_waspas: After linear normalisation the weighted sum (WSM) and weighted product (WPM) are calculated and joined with λ.
ipucu.y_edas: Each criterion's average (AV) is found; distances above (PDA) and below (NDA) the average in the good direction are weighted. A higher appraisal score AS is better.
ipucu.y_copras: Values are divided by the column sum and weighted. Benefit (S⁺) and cost (S⁻) sums are kept separately; a higher relative significance Q is better. The utility degree is a percentage of the best.
ipucu.y_moora: After vector normalisation, weighted benefit values are added and cost values subtracted. A higher y* is better.
ipucu.y_aras: An optimal alternative made of each criterion's best value is added. Each alternative's total is divided by the optimal one; the closer the utility degree K is to 1, the better.
ipucu.y_mabac: A border area (G) is found for each criterion as the geometric mean of the alternatives. A higher total distance S from this border is better.
ipucu.y_marcos: Ideal (AI) and anti-ideal (AAI) solutions are added to the matrix. The alternatives' utility degrees relative to them (K⁺, K⁻) are combined in a utility function; a higher f(K) is better.
ipucu.y_saw: The weighted sum of linearly normalised values. The simplest method and a reference point for the others.
